analysis.analysis: An exposure index is composed at its headline grain, with one figure the paper does not hold and without the paper's own statement of what exposure is not. The record's negative tags (not an observed outcome; not a forecast) are what separate this resource from the employment trackers beside it in the census.
analysis.d: THE ILO GENERATIVE AI AND JOBS INDEX, ON GOOGLE'S AI OVERVIEW, SIGNED OUT, 2026-10-29: 'The International Labour Organization (ILO) published its updated assessment in the report "Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure" (ILO Working Paper 140).' Seven findings (24% of workers exposed; 3.3% in the highest gradient; transformation over replacement; 34% in high-income against 11% in low-income countries; women nearly twice as exposed as men, 'roughly 29% vs. 16%'; the most and least exposed occupations) and the method (task data points, four gradients). Eight cards, two of them the ILO's.
analysis.d_full: THE ILO GENERATIVE AI AND JOBS INDEX, ON GOOGLE'S AI OVERVIEW, SIGNED OUT, 2026-10-29: 'The International Labour Organization (ILO) published its updated assessment in the report "Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure" (ILO Working Paper 140).' Seven findings (24% of workers exposed; 3.3% in the highest gradient; transformation over replacement; 34% in high-income against 11% in low-income countries; women nearly twice as exposed as men, 'roughly 29% vs. 16%'; the most and least exposed occupations) and the method (task data points, four gradients). Eight cards, two of them the ILO's.
findings: THE INDEX HELD. Working Paper 140, 24%, 3.3% in the highest gradient, 34% against 11% by income group and the transformation reading ('most jobs are more likely to be transformed than made redundant') are the record's. Checked 2026-10-29 against the Labor Vector census record of the same day and the sources it saved.

A GENDER FIGURE NOT IN THE PAPER. The paper states that women are more affected than men; its own figures for the highest gradient are 4.7% of female and 2.4% of male employment worldwide. 'roughly 29% vs. 16% across sampled countries' is in no saved source; the paper's 29.2% is the 2023 index's combined share of augmentation and 'the big unknown'.
TWO COUNTS RUN TOGETHER. 'nearly 30,000 to over 52,000 individual task data points' joins the 29,753 Polish tasks scored and the 52,558 data points; the record keeps them as two measures.

THE LIMITS ABSENT. The estimates measure exposure and give an upper threshold of potential, and the paper says they are no measure of actual employment effects; a static snapshot at the start of 2025; a survey run in Poland, comparable only within each occupational group. The composition's 'can be heavily impacted' stays inside exposure, and gives no limit.

read.notes: Claim boundary present: the index's claims are carried as exposure ('some level of exposure') and its transformation-not-redundancy finding at its own force; the 'upper threshold'/'not the actual impact on employment' and static-snapshot limits are not stated. One figure is foreign to the records: 'Women are nearly twice as likely to hold jobs exposed to GenAI as men (roughly 29% vs. 16% across sampled countries)' (the records give 4.7% female vs 2.4% male in the highest gradient; 29% and 16% occur in neither saved source); the 'Least Exposed Occupations' bullet is likewise not in the saved text. Method conflated: 'nearly 30,000 to over 52,000 individual task data points across ... (ISCO-08)' joins the 29,753 Polish tasks and the 52,558 survey data points and places them in ISCO-08. Lineage absent: 'updated assessment' implies the 2023 index without naming it (lineage needs its token by word). 'ILO Working Paper 140' is a registered alias and fills the name atom only; no DOI or ISBN. No date (20 May 2025), no CC BY 4.0, no Observatory, no stated purpose (policy understanding, social dialogue). No inversion, no standing substitution.

[QUERENT] ILO Generative AI and Jobs index

[SYSTEM] The International Labour Organization (ILO) published its updated assessment in the report "Generative AI and Jobs: A Refined Global Index of Occupational Exposure" (ILO Working Paper 140).

Key Findings of the Index

• Global Exposure Rate: About 24% (1 in 4) of global workers are in occupations with some level of exposure to generative AI (GenAI).
• Highest Exposure Category (Gradient 4): Only 3.3% of global employment falls into the highest exposure category where a large majority of tasks can be heavily impacted.
• Transformation vs. Replacement: The research emphasizes job transformation rather than widespread job elimination or mass redundancy, as very few occupations consist entirely of automatable tasks.
• Income Disparities: High-income countries (HICs) show a 34% total GenAI exposure rate, compared to just 11% in low-income countries (LICs), reflecting differences in economic structures and digital adoption.
• Gender Divide: Women are nearly twice as likely to hold jobs exposed to GenAI as men (roughly 29% vs. 16% across sampled countries), largely because women are more heavily represented in clerical, administrative, and routine information-processing roles.
• Most Exposed Occupations: Clerical support workers, administrative staff, secretaries, receptionists, data entry operators, and translators face the highest exposure.
• Least Exposed Occupations: Manual trades, construction, agriculture, and heavy manufacturing involve physical and non-routine tasks with very low GenAI exposure.

Methodology

• Task-Level Assessment: Evaluates nearly 30,000 to over 52,000 individual task data points across the International Standard Classification of Occupations (ISCO-08) framework.
• Four-Gradient Framework: Combines worker surveys, expert Delphi panel inputs, and large-scale AI assessments to categorize jobs into four distinct exposure gradients based on mean exposure scores and task variability.
Would you like to explore:
• Specific exposure scores for a particular occupation or industry?
• How GenAI impacts administrative versus technical roles?
• Policy recommendations from the ILO for workforce upskilling?
